Pytrees

Source: vignettes/pytrees.Rmd
pytrees.Rmd
library(jaxR)

A pytree is a nested container of arrays: the parameters of a model, the state of an optimizer, a batch of data. Every transformation in jaxR accepts pytrees wherever it accepts arrays. In R, the pytree containers are lists (named or not), NULL (a tree with no leaves) and classes registered with the functions of this vignette. Everything else is a leaf.

params <- list(
  dense = list(w = jnp_ones(c(2L, 3L)), b = jnp_zeros(3L)),
  scale = as_jax(2))

Pytrees in transformations

grad returns a tree with the structure of its argument:

loss <- function(p, x) jnp_sum((x %*% p$dense$w + p$dense$b)^2) * p$scale
g <- grad(loss)(params, jnp_ones(c(4L, 2L)))
str(lapply(g$dense, dim))
#> List of 2
#>  $ w: int [1:2] 2 3
#>  $ b: int 3
g$scale
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 48

vmap maps over the leading axis of every leaf, jit flattens arguments and results, and control flow carries pytrees as loop state:

batch <- list(a = jnp_reshape(jnp_arange(6, dtype = "float32"), c(3L, 2L)), b = as_jax(c(1, 2, 3)))
vmap(function(el) jnp_sum(el$a) * el$b)(batch)
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1]  1 10 27

lax_fori_loop(0L, 3L, function(i, s) list(n = s$n + 1L, total = s$total + i),
              list(n = 0L, total = 0L))
#> $n
#> Array i32[] weak_type
#> [1] 3
#> 
#> $total
#> Array i32[]
#> [1] 3

Working with trees 

tree_leaves(params)
#> [[1]]
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 0 0 0
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> Array f32[2,3]
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    1    1
#> [2,]    1    1    1
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 2
tree_structure(params)
#> PyTreeDef(list(dense = list(w = *, b = *), scale = *))
tree_map(function(x) x * 0, params)$dense$b
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 0 0 0
tree_map(function(x, y) x + y, list(1, list(2, 3)), list(10, list(20, 30)))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 11
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [[2]][[1]]
#> [1] 22
#> 
#> [[2]][[2]]
#> [1] 33
tree_reduce(function(acc, x) acc + jnp_size(x), params, 0L)
#> [1] 10
tree_all(tree_map(function(x) jnp_all(jnp_isfinite(x)), params))
#> [1] TRUE

tree_flatten and tree_unflatten are the inverse pair underneath:

fl <- tree_flatten(params)
length(fl$leaves)
#> [1] 3
rebuilt <- tree_unflatten(fl$treedef, lapply(fl$leaves, function(x) x + 1))
rebuilt$scale
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 3

Named lists flatten in sorted key order, as Python dictionaries do in JAX, so two trees with the same names in a different order have the same leaves order:

tree_leaves(list(b = 2, a = 1))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 2

is_leaf stops the traversal early:

length(tree_leaves(params, is_leaf = function(x) is.list(x) && !is.null(x$w)))
#> [1] 2

Paths 

kl <- tree_leaves_with_path(params)
vapply(kl, function(p) keystr(p[[1]]), "")
#> [1] "['dense']['b']" "['dense']['w']" "['scale']"
vapply(kl, function(p) keystr(p[[1]], simple = TRUE, separator = "/"), "")
#> [1] "dense/b" "dense/w" "scale"
tree_map_with_path(function(path, x) paste(keystr(path), jnp_size(x)), params)$dense$w
#> [1] "['dense']['w'] 6"

Path entries are DictKey, SequenceKey, GetAttrKey and FlattenedIndexKey objects.

Structure utilities 

# A list of two records becomes a record of two lists
outer <- tree_structure(list(0, 0))
inner <- tree_structure(list(x = 0, y = 0))
tree_transpose(outer, inner, list(list(x = 1, y = 2), list(x = 3, y = 4)))
#> $x
#> $x[[1]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $x[[2]]
#> [1] 3
#> 
#> 
#> $y
#> $y[[1]]
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> $y[[2]]
#> [1] 4

tree_broadcast(list(1, 2), list(list(3, 4), list(a = 5, b = 6)))
#> [[1]]
#> [[1]][[1]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> [[1]][[2]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [[2]]$a
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> [[2]]$b
#> [1] 2

td <- tree_structure(params)
treedef_num_leaves(td)
#> [1] 3
length(treedef_children(td))
#> [1] 2

ravel_pytree flattens a tree of arrays to one vector and returns the inverse, which is what optimizers that work on a flat vector need:

rv <- ravel_pytree(params)
dim(rv[[1]])
#> [1] 10
str(lapply(rv[[2]](rv[[1]] * 2)$dense, dim))
#> List of 2
#>  $ w: int [1:2] 2 3
#>  $ b: int 3

Registering classes

An S3 object is a leaf until its class is registered. register_pytree_node takes the class name, a flatten function returning list(children =, aux =) and an unflatten function.

new_gaussian <- function(mean, sd, label) {
  structure(list(mean = mean, sd = sd, label = label), class = "gaussian")
}
register_pytree_node("gaussian",
  function(x) list(children = list(x$mean, x$sd), aux = x$label),
  function(aux, children) new_gaussian(children[[1]], children[[2]], aux))

d <- new_gaussian(as_jax(0), as_jax(1), "prior")
tree_leaves(d)
#> [[1]]
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 1
nll <- function(d, x) -jnp_sum(scipy_stats_norm_logpdf(x, d$mean, d$sd))
g <- grad(nll)(d, as_jax(c(0.5, 1.5)))
class(g)
#> [1] "gaussian"
g$mean
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] -2

For a list based class, register_dataclass is shorter: name the fields that hold arrays and the fields that are static metadata.

register_dataclass("layer", data_fields = c("w", "b"), meta_fields = "activation")
l <- structure(list(w = jnp_ones(2L), b = as_jax(0), activation = "relu"), class = "layer")
vapply(tree_leaves_with_path(l), function(p) keystr(p[[1]]), "")
#> [1] ".w" ".b"

register_pytree_with_keys also records the path entry of each child, and register_static declares a class with no leaves (configuration objects that pass through transformations untouched). register_pytree_node_class and register_pytree_with_keys_class look up the methods tree_flatten.<class> and tree_unflatten.<class> by name.

Partial

jax_Partial(f, ...) binds leading arguments, like functools.partial. The result is a pytree whose leaves are the bound arguments, so it can be passed through jit and vmap as data.

scale_by <- jax_Partial(function(k, x) k * x, as_jax(3))
scale_by(as_jax(c(1, 2)))
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1] 3 6
tree_leaves(scale_by)
#> [[1]]
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 3
jit(function(f, x) f(x))(scale_by, as_jax(c(1, 2)))
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1] 3 6

NULL and static leaves

NULL is a tree without leaves, so optional parts of a structure can be absent. R values that are not arrays (strings, functions) are leaves; transformations reject them as array arguments, so keep them in aux data or in a registered static class.

tree_leaves(list(1, NULL, list(NULL, 2)))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 2
